claim: The back-of-napkin lifetime calculation

title: Million Dollar Equations
claim: Gross profit, not revenue

title: Million Dollar Equations
claim: Return on invested capital at the location level
context: For brick-and-mortar, the customer-level ratio is not enough — you need the all-in cost to open a location (marketing, buildout, hiring, ads) and then three outputs: payback period, one-year return, and cash flow at capacity. He wants at least 3:1 and ideally 5:1 on that capital.

title: Million Dollar Equations
claim: Four levers to shorten payback
context: Get first and last month up front; charge a mandatory fee (onboarding, enrolment, setup); add an optional upsell (functionally the same as the fee); or bring in a third-party financier who fronts the contract for a cut and takes the risk.

title: Million Dollar Equations
claim: Sales velocity x LTGP (the hypothetical max)
context: Units sold per month times lifetime gross profit (or LTV) tells you where the business evens out if nothing else changes — the steady state it is already heading toward, which is why a $500k/month business can be a doubling business and a $2M/month one a shrinking business.

title: Million Dollar Equations
claim: Sales velocity ÷ churn (the customer ceiling)
context: How many customers the business will have to service at steady state, which tells you whether current infrastructure is over- or under-built and when headcount decisions become unavoidable.

title: Million Dollar Equations
claim: TAM ÷ risk
context: Potential units times lifetime gross profit divided by risk — his top-level opportunity equation. He calls TAM important but barely knowable, and puts it in the Munger/Buffett 'important but unknown' box, which is why he only tries to price knowable risk.

title: Million Dollar Equations
claim: Knowable and important

title: Million Dollar Equations
claim: Narrow then expand
context: The reason a small TAM is not fatal: most big companies start with a narrow avatar and redefine the market later — Amazon began as a bookstore, Facebook as a social network for college students.

claim: Valuation effect of cutting a cost centre
context: A fast-growing company that removes an entire massive cost centre — marketing — while gaining instant national recognition starts at a much higher valuation on day one, because both growth and margin are better than a comparable consumer brand.

title: Why MrBeast Will be Worth $100 Billion
claim: Hire the god squad
context: MrBeast's talent strategy as he describes it: recruit the best business and content people in-house, including having them move into his house to absorb the way of doing things, because smart people want to board a fast-growing ship.

title: Goal Setting

title: Goal Setting

title: Goal Setting

title: Goal Setting

title: Goal Setting
claim: Goal setting should take work
context: The process is diagnostic: if you can knock your goals out quickly, you have probably not thought them through, because the framework forces you to articulate why you are doing what you are doing at all.

value: a 10-year relationship cited as what he respects when partners talk about their counterparties
context: his stated test for how a business owner talks about the people they do deals with

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: He who gives the money has the power
context: The person supplying capital dictates terms; wanting money puts you in the weak seat. He points at banks as the biggest institutions in the world whose whole business is giving money.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Never trade reputation for money
context: Money can be recovered, reputation cannot. Reputation is the compounding asset that lets you do more deals, bigger deals, faster — and trading it for short-term money cuts the compounding.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Money loves speed, wealth loves time, poverty loves indecision
context: Speed wins at the transaction level (follow up on leads, serve customers fast), but building wealth requires letting compounding run uninterrupted — and most people never achieve either because they stay in indecision.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: We can always make more money than we need
context: The belief that removes scarcity from decisions: he and Leila have never gone without food or shelter and have kept increasing their skill set, so they can take risks without the animal brain deciding from fear.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Change the behaviour once you have the castle
context: The behaviour that builds a fortune (bet everything, nothing to lose) is the behaviour that destroys it once you have something to lose — so the risk posture has to be swapped, not doubled down.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Money flows where attention goes
context: Where your attention sits is where money accumulates; pick one thing and go all in, because the magnifying-glass effect requires concentrating heat on one spot to burn through to the next level.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Align home and business money rules
context: You cannot reinvest everything in a business while living lavishly at home. He and Leila run the same rules in both: no debt personally, no debt in the business.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Ignore money advice from poor people
context: Stated more precisely: ignore money advice from parents, friends or anyone with smaller dreams for your life than you have — because people who can lose everything and recreate it see reality more accurately.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: All the slow on the buy, all the lubricant on the sell
context: It is always easier to buy than to sell, so put friction into acquisition decisions and remove friction from exits — buying is instant and selling requires a counterparty.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Frugality drives innovation
context: Constraint — of time or money — forces creative problem solving instead of buying the answer, which is exactly what people who have money try to recreate deliberately.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Investing vs spending
context: Investing is money that returns something later — a skill that raises earning capacity, or yield/appreciation. Spending is money on something that will never be worth more in the future because it is consumed.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Money flows to the person who needs it least
context: The rich get richer because they do not need the money, and not needing it is the leverage. Sell from the buyer's wallet, not your own, and come to the table with other options.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: We make money, our money does not make us
context: Tying self-worth to net worth turns the net worth into a liability to your self-esteem — and wealth can be taken (his family lost everything in the Iranian Revolution), so the durable asset is the ability to make money.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: It may be an amazing opportunity, but not our amazing opportunity
context: The permission-to-decline mechanism: once you get past analysis paralysis, the yes muscle over-flexes and you must be able to say no to good opportunities that are not yours.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Control the money flow upstream
context: The further upstream you sit in the payment chain, the more leverage and control you have — banks get the money and give it back later, and everyone looks brilliant until the day they cannot process money.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Oh-shit fund
context: Enough set aside that you are protected no matter what risk you take. Having it changes your posture from defensive to offensive, which is why he says to build it as early as possible.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: The biggest eroder of wealth is ignorance
context: Not knowing how to make money costs you the gap between your income and a million every year — an invisible hand suppressing income, which is why he pays to learn.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: FOMO means go slow
context: When he feels FOMO he pauses: the feeling comes from too short a time horizon, and mistakes love a rushed decision. Slowing down has saved him a lot of money.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Leverage comes from needing nothing
context: You cannot influence someone who needs nothing — the monks achieve it by relinquishing everything, the rich man by satisfying all his needs and not needing the deal on the other side of the table.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Markets take longer to adjust than you expect, then move faster than you can imagine
context: The Big Short trade was early for about four years before the move happened instantly; the requirement is being comfortable sitting in discomfort before your view of reality is reflected.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Money is a game — treat it as such
context: You cannot win a game you do not know you are playing. The wealthiest treat it as a scoreboard with personal bests, because what gets measured gets improved — his example is people losing weight just by weighing themselves daily with no other advice.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Don't bet the empire for a pot of gold
context: Never risk the whole pie for one opportunity: you can go all in with your attention but not with your money, because losing the empire ends the game.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Starter deal with new faces
context: With friends, new partners or new counterparties, do a small first deal. Everything can look great on paper and the person can be excellent, and you still cap the downside by starting small.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Trust is worth more than a bigger return
context: Trust lubricates deal velocity and compounds, so do not take all the meat on the bone — leave room for the long-term relationship. How a person talks about their existing partners tells you how they will do business with you.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Never take a standard deal
context: There is always a better deal and it usually requires asking for it, naming the concerning terms, and being willing to walk away — which works because leverage comes from not needing the deal.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Expect low risk, amazing returns
context: His billionaire friends look for 50%+ annualized, not the 10% the S&P does; the market average is not a personal standard, and that reframe changed how he invests.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Diversification is a hedge against ignorance
context: Credited to Buffett: spreading across stocks, real estate, crypto and side hustles prevents getting good at any of them, because you are competing with people who play one game all in.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Returns are in the terms
context: The terms of an agreement determine what you can make; learning to structure terms in many different ways is a skill acquired through conversations and other people's deals.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: House money
context: Whenever possible recoup your principal and leave the rest in the game, so you can be aggressive with no chance of losing principal.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Always know how to get your money back
context: Not a vague belief that you can get it back — the exact steps, walked through one by one. If the counterparty does not mean it, they will not have a way to do it.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Cash flow is king
context: Income minus expenses, measured at the level of what you save every month rather than what you make — the metric switch he says is the one takeaway of the video.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Buy for forever
context: A Mungerism he quotes: the money is not made in the buy or the sell, it is made in the wait. If you could never sell, you would buy differently — and that is what keeps compounding uninterrupted.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: If you can't afford to lose the money, don't use the money
context: If it is your last dollar, do not risk it — which is exactly what the oh-shit fund exists to prevent.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Peace of mind can be bought and sold
context: If a decision will keep you up at night, don't do it; you make better decisions when you have peace of mind, and it is a purchasable input.

title: 42 Recession-Proof Money Secrets
claim: Diversify across the capital stack, not just industries
context: Everyone diversifies by industry and forgets where they sit vertically in the capital stack. Banks are preferred creditors, which is why they rarely lose money — so when the tide goes out, sit where you get paid first.

title: Hard work will not make you rich

title: Hard work will not make you rich

context: His method for growing a business: look at what the CEO spends time on, identify the low-leverage activities, hand them to someone else on the org chart, and where an entire category of activity has no owner, hire that role.

title: Hard work will not make you rich

context: A quest needs a party with complementary skills — healer, mage, paladin — not ten copies of the same class. Same for football: you do not field ten running backs, and the entrepreneur who tries to be the star player loses to the company that has a team.

title: Hard work will not make you rich

context: The replacement for the outwork brag: no one can out-recruit me, out-manage me, or build a culture like me — high-leverage claims across the whole organisation instead of an activity metric.

title: Hard work will not make you rich
claim: The four levels of the entrepreneur
context: Player (pick a position on the field), specialist (CMO, chief sales officer, chief product officer), coach (headhunt and recruit the best players), and dynasty-builder (recruit top executives and build a farm system that feeds the company).

title: Hard work will not make you rich
claim: The value of the coach is the delta
context: Ask what the players would do with no coach, then what they would do with the best coach — the difference between those two outcomes is the value of the coach, and the same delta across an organisation is the CEO's leverage.

title: Hard work will not make you rich
claim: Highest return on time in the organisation
context: The CEO must have the highest return on time of anyone, because their job is always to be solving the next problem — and the trade works as long as what they move to builds the business more than what they gave up.

title: Hard work will not make you rich
claim: Leverage that keeps selling
context: Writing a book is his example of the leverage term: spend the time once and the book prints and sells copies forever, which is a different way to play the same game.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: Price anchoring
context: Show the most expensive option first so every other price is judged against it. The anchor works two ways: it stretches the range through which buyers see your pricing, and it anchors the rest of the menu downward.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: Put the most expensive option first
context: On any membership or pricing menu, lead with the most expensive option, not the cheapest — everything else then looks cheaper by comparison. He says it works on wine, software, memberships, anything, because it works on psychology.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: The 10x/50x/100x menu
context: Whatever you sell, create a version 10, 50 or 100 times more expensive, then work out what you would have to fulfil to make it worth that price. The exercise also teaches you that people will spend more when they see the value.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: Great deals, not cheap stuff
context: Price is what you pay, value is what you get, and the deal is the discrepancy between the two. People want to buy great deals — which is why the middle option at $9 against a $10 large outsells the cheap one.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: They can't afford it is a value problem
context: If a buyer believed you were giving them a Ferrari for $10,000 they would find the money — so the reason someone does not buy something expensive is that they do not understand the value, not that the money does not exist.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: Whales buy the most expensive thing
context: Some percentage of people always buy the cheapest thing and another percentage always buy the most expensive. Having a very expensive item on the menu costs nothing, serves that second group, and surprises you when it sells.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: Break the rubber band of pricing
context: If the price does not get a gasp, it is not high enough. The gasp shows you have broken the range the buyer associated with your product — after which the real offer looks reasonable by comparison.

title: How to Sell Anything

context: Tiers set $10 apart ($100/$110/$120) fail because the customers between them are the same person. Price tiers to different avatars and different needs instead, so the ladder maps to who is buying.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: Price to the value of the specific avatar
context: The same service is worth more to a bigger customer — a conversion-rate service is worth 10x more to a $100M/year store than to a $1M/year store, because the value delivered depends on who they are, not who you are.

title: How to Sell Anything
claim: The expensive anchor is not the product, it is the frame
context: The top-priced option exists to make everything below it feel like a bargain — he says to put it there expecting never to sell it, then be surprised when you do.

In the real world you cash out and keep the money; in the casino of life the grim reaper taps your shoulder, all your chips are pushed back to the middle, and you leave empty-handed because it was a fake game with fake rules.

title: The Bigger the Monster, the Greater the Hero
claim: Death taxes everybody
context: The land he bought in Austin had owners before him who called it theirs and died or sold it — so property is just chips being amassed and redistributed. Estate planning is therefore an attempt to control something that always reverts.

title: The Bigger the Monster, the Greater the Hero

title: The Bigger the Monster, the Greater the Hero

title: The Bigger the Monster, the Greater the Hero

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Level 1 - I work, then you pay
context: Standard W-2 employment: you trade risk for reliability and get paid regardless of outcome. He rejects the claim that employment is riskier than owning a business - if that were true everyone would own one.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Level 2 - You pay as we go
context: Payment runs in parallel with work - half now, half later, or by milestone. Typical for contractors and vendors, with the caveat that people fire vendors five times faster than employees.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Level 3 - You pay, then I work
context: Paid in full up front before work begins, which he says you can only do when you own a business - surgeons and attorneys on retainer are the examples. Where you sit on this pyramid tells you your leverage.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Business owner layaway
context: A level-three structure: let the buyer invent their own payment plan, then tell them work starts only once it is paid off. It converts 'I can't afford it' into 'I'll pay faster', and if they default you keep everything already paid.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Level 4 - When X happens, you pay me
context: Rev share, profit share, outcome-based bonus, accelerators and equity all share this shape: compensation is divorced from time worked and attached to an outcome, which is predicated on skill.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Compensated in proportion to perceived risk
context: The through-line of the whole video: you get paid in proportion to the risk you are willing to take on - specifically the perceived risk. The people who do this well take risk that is very risky to others and not risky to them, and the market overpays for that.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Mispriced bets
context: What investors call it when the market overpays you for risk you can price better than it can - the mechanism behind every level above three.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Level 5 - Buy and sell risk itself
context: Insurance: you are paid every month nothing happens, and the nothing that happened becomes profit. There is no delivery beyond the agreement to carry the risk, which is why insurance predates the tax code and why the oldest companies in the world are insurers.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Insurance is a reverse lottery
context: Everyone buys a ticket and if the bad thing happens to one of them, everyone else chips in.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Level 6 - No matter what you pay me (control of the money flow)
context: The top level: get paid because you control the money as it moves. Franchisors who collect and remit, payment processors who take their slice in transit, and the tax collector - who is paid no matter what because the government holds a monopoly on violence.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Royalties come off the top
context: The word royalty comes from payments to the royals: it means paid first and off the top. Rev share beats profit share because profit can be played with and revenue cannot.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: The longevity razor
context: When evaluating a business model, look at the companies that have survived longest - a company that has been around 100 plus years has proven it knows how to take on risk and be paid for it.

title: The 6 Levels of Making Money
claim: Sell the guarantee without being the insurer
context: You can inject risk-taking into any business - a guarantee, a warranty, a promise to absorb delays or difficulty - and charge a premium for it. AppleCare is his example.

title: You can make way more money than you think

title: You can make way more money than you think
claim: The four business-model shapes

title: You can make way more money than you think
claim: Demand-constrained versus supply-constrained

title: You can make way more money than you think

title: You can make way more money than you think

context: When you are 85 and split between two choices, pick the cooler story - because the hard thing is usually the right thing, and if the easy thing were right you would already have done it.

title: How to Become Ultra Wealthy (4 Methods)
claim: A private equity fund - the fourth path, other people's money into other people's businesses. Modelled on American Pacific Group, the $500 million fund that bought his own companies in 2021 for $46.2 million.
value: Worked over 10 years: $300 million of businesses triples to $900 million. Less $200 million of debt, $100 million returned to LPs and roughly $100 million of interest leaves $500 million. The 20% carry is $100 million, which is $80 million post-tax. Add the $20 million of management fees and the GP turns a $5 million slug into $100 million plus over the period - and he notes that on a $2 billion fund you simply multiply by 20.
context: The highest-leverage capital structure is not owning a business or investing in one - it is controlling other people's capital invested in other people's businesses, because three layers of leverage stack on a small personal stake: LP capital on top of GP capital, debt on top of equity, and the acquired companies' cash flow on top of the debt. The GP is paid twice, once on assets raised regardless of outcome and once on profit, and the profit portion is taxed as capital gains. The prerequisite is not capital but access - proprietary deal flow plus an industry edge - which is why the same model is unavailable to a passive investor no matter how much money they have.

Supply-constrained (cleaning, accounting, legal, consulting) means the real business is recruiting, hiring, training and incentivising. title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026
claim: The media and conversion team inside acquisition.com - the division that produces his content and runs the acquisition funnel. He took direct control of it in the reporting year after about five years away from day-to-day operating.
value: Output more than doubled, with the expectation of reaching triple or quadruple. Separately, the largest portfolio company produced three CRO wins in the year - 20%, 50% and 28% lifts - off roughly 100 split tests run by one person and a couple of developers, at a company doing eight figures plus per month in revenue. Across the portfolio, EBITDA went from $50 million to just under $100 million.
context: When a function is underperforming, delete before you optimise and optimise before you automate. Remove every recurring time block first and let the ones that matter be re-added by demand rather than assumed by habit. Then attach a time estimate to every task and pull it up, because unused bandwidth is not preserved - the future will not resemble today. Finally, change the reward structure, because the constraint is usually not capability but incentive: if the only way to advance is headcount, the org will manufacture hiring requests and manage for visibility instead of output. Back-test any new comp plan against the previous month before adopting it, and let incumbents keep their salary with performance added on top so the transition is adopted rather than resisted.

title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL
claim: United Fitness - his own chain of gyms, opened with no capital by having customers prepay and finance each new location.
value: Six locations by age 25, opened on a six-month cadence with essentially no capital out of pocket. The model was then productised: Gym Launch 1.0 charged $100,000 per gym on $1,000-$5,000 of ad spend, running 32+ launches in about 18 months; the licensing version went 0 to $10 million in sales in 10 months and did $26 million topline with about $16 million EBITDA in its second full year.
context: When capital is the constraint, change the timing of cash rather than raising money. Sell a finite, outcome-shaped commitment (a six-week challenge) instead of an open-ended membership so the customer pays before you deliver; price the front-end so the first transaction returns more than the cost of the customer plus the cost of goods plus the cost of the next customer; and sequence the buildout so each week's collections fund the next week's spend. The test to manage to is 2x CAC + COGS collected within 30 days, because 30 days is the interest-free window on a credit card - which means the cycle can repeat without a lender.

title: I Lost $100 Million... Here's What I Learned
claim: Red flags are red flags - believe them the first time

title: I Lost $100 Million... Here's What I Learned
claim: Push or pivot
context: Some hard moments require pushing through; others mean your fundamental assumption was wrong and you must change direction. The mistake is doing neither - coasting.

title: I Lost $100 Million... Here's What I Learned
claim: More, better, new - in that order
context: His anti-distraction rule, born from repeatedly losing money by splitting focus onto a smaller pile instead of doubling down on the big one.

title: I Lost $100 Million... Here's What I Learned
claim: Know where the bodies are buried
context: You don't need to know everything, but you do need one layer deeper on every department's current problems, or someone can execute a company-wide change without you knowing.

title: I Lost $100 Million... Here's What I Learned
claim: References like you
context: When vetting a vendor or hire, demand references from someone with your exact use case and size - and then treat a personal referral as a stranger from that point forward.

title: I Lost $100 Million... Here's What I Learned
claim: Listen to customers, not competitors
context: His rule after the pricing disaster: competitors are largely irrelevant if you are paying attention to customers. He attributes the phrasing to Paul Graham.

title: I Lost $100 Million... Here's What I Learned
claim: Hormozi's own portfolio of ventures over ~a decade: crypto, single-family rental, gyms, gym licensing (Gym Launch), a meal company, a software company (Allen) and various vendor relationships. Presented as a personal loss ledger rather than a balance sheet.
value: Cumulative stated loss $100 million across the career. Named line items include $15 million on the vendor launch failure, $10-25 million on the food-business distraction (including the lost exit multiple), $5 million per year of profit permanently lost to the price cut, $1.2 million on delegated compliance, $1 million+ on outsourced software, $600,000/year on the unauthorised raise, $500,000 on crypto, and a $30-50k lesson from a single Ohio house.
context: Losses cluster into two repeatable causes that have nothing to do with market conditions: leaving the domain where you have developed skill, and diverting focus from the business with the highest return on your time. Both are self-inflicted and both are cheap to avoid - the discipline is a written rule about what you will not do, not better analysis of the thing you want to do. The corollary for pricing: never cut price reactively, because 20% off the topline at 40% margins is 50% of profit, and that recurring profit is what your eventual sale multiple is applied to.

title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

context: Most outcomes are like a pipeline with several valves: they do not occur until every condition is met, so partial effort produces nothing and the correct response is to find the missing condition rather than to call it unfair.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: The champion wall
context: The point where excitement fades and work actually begins - that is where everyone else stops, and where the gap opens. Work begins once motivation stops.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: Education as investment, not expense
context: Stop using poor-people language about education and use investor language: there is only a cost and a return, and the asset happens to be you - you cannot sell it but you can invest in it and grow it.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: Model what they did, not what happened
context: Overnight success is a threshold: the public sees the viral moment, not the inputs. Most people get rich and then get weird, and people copy the weird part - you don't get rich by flying private jets, you fly private jets after you get rich.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: End of day, not end of week
context: Collapse deadlines: ask 'can I get it done by end of today' instead of end of week, then end of hour. A 7x and then further compression in your pace of progress.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: Masters have more ways to win
context: You can measure expertise by the number of ways you can measure progress - an expert has many intermediate win markers on a long project, a beginner only sees the final output and therefore sees nothing happening.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: The bricks and the bridge
context: Education is bricks on a road to a goal. People who already bought a brick elsewhere have no gap, so the same programme works for them and fails for you - and nobody calls a house foundation a ripoff.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: It takes what it takes
context: His and Leila's internal saying: the real world is an auction of trade-offs, not a fixed price. You keep bidding - 30, then 50, then 100, then 300 - until you own it, and only then does everyone say you were born good.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: Act with urgency (the thought-to-action gap)
context: You can tell how successful someone will be by the gap between thought and action. The extreme is the god figure where thought and reality are one; you approximate it by shrinking the delay, and 'decide' literally means to cut off alternatives.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%
claim: Sword of Gryffindor
context: Only take in that which makes you stronger. Applied to bad coaching experiences and vendors: instead of enumerating what they did wrong, ask in what way this makes you better - do everything they say to the tea the first time, then take what works and toss the rest.

context: A skill that helps you acquire more skills - learning how to learn is the meta skill. title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday
claim: Reward, punish, extinguish
context: Teaching is training, and training is only three levers: what you reward, what you punish, and what you extinguish by doing nothing. title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday
claim: Brand as a bouquet of associations
context: A brand exists to change the behaviour of your target audience, and you build it by pairing things they don't know (your logo, tagline, company) with things they do know and like. title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

Own fulfilment AND the customer, or the channel in the middle will refund your sales. Stack processing capacity the way you stack offers. And when you shut something down, write every check - the clean exit is what lets the next model get sold.

context: The order in which people get paid when money flows - whoever is paid earliest has the most control and makes the most money. Rungs bottom to top: employee (fronts labour, paid 2-4 weeks later), self-employed (fronts or splits 50/50), paid first (doctor, professional), banks (preferred creditors who take the defined pot and leave the scraps), insurance (paid the whole time and may never have to perform), God (10% off the top for life).

claim: Price divided by churn equals LTV (the four levers)
context: Price ÷ churn = LTV, then traffic × conversion applied to it. Price is bidirectional — raising it lowers conversion and raises churn — so every price decision is a simultaneous bet on all four levers. You are optimising earnings per click over the longest period.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: LTV to CAC times TAM
context: The avatar-selection test: the ratio of what a customer is worth to what they cost to acquire, multiplied by the size of the market. He uses it to tell a hair-salon owner to drop a 11:1 coaching offer for a 24:1 product offer in a much larger market.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Big head, long tail (one-time value vs ongoing consumable value)
context: Separate the one-time value you deliver (education, blueprints, tools — permanent value, price it up front) from the ongoing consumable value (community, calls, ad testing, done-for-you services — price it monthly). His diagnosis of the education industry is that it bundles both into one payment plan spread over a year, so the value collapses the day the customer learns the skill while the payments continue.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: The value decay curve (why payment plans over a year create churn)
context: Value delivered up front and price paid over time diverge: the day after someone learns to run Facebook ads, the value of the content teaching Facebook ads is zero, but the payments keep coming. That gap is where churn comes from.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: More, better, new — in that order
context: Before trying anything new, argue why you cannot simply do more of what already works, then why you cannot do it better. New is the last resort, because finding something that works is the hard part and most small operators find something that works and then abandon it for six new things.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Saying no to money (the discipline that creates focus)
context: The scarce resource is attention, not revenue, so the highest-leverage act is refusing money that pulls you off the one thing. He paid $2 million in refunds to concentrate on a single business, and cites the sting of that refund as the thing that makes later refusals easy.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: The friendly goodbye (Planet Fitness retention model)
context: Make the exit frictionless and warm rather than punitive, because the market is finite and you will cycle through the entire town repeatedly. A 'you can never come back' rule does nothing for communities with weak retention and nothing for strong ones either, since a strong community is already the reason people stay.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Overwhelm is the main cause of churn
context: The instinct to keep adding to a community is backwards. Consumption has to be the highest priority, which means removing modules, cutting calls and shortening the offer until people can actually get through it — Skool hides the classroom tab for new communities because making a course has no correlation with retention.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Lifetime deals are one-time income with forever delivery
context: The structural flaw in selling lifetime access: you collect once and owe delivery in perpetuity, which makes it impossible to change avatar or offer later. His remedy is to refund rather than serve out a deal you no longer want.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Maker time versus manager time
context: Makers need whole blocks — about 14 a week, one morning and one afternoon slot per day — and losing one costs a fourteenth of the week. Managers work in 15-minute increments and can spread across 20 slots a day. The damage is when managers interrupt makers. His own answer was six meeting-free hours every morning since he was poor.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Hiring is the same funnel as customer acquisition
context: Generate applications, nurture applications, the interview is the sale, onboarding, then retain or ascend. Scaling is when the inflow of talent matches the inflow of customers, and brand counts twice — once on the front end for customers and again on the back end for talent.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Direction is inversely proportional to skill
context: The less skilled the person, the more specific the instructions must be; the more skilled, the less you have to say. He describes telling a top operator 'just promote it' while a junior needs copy, hooks and emails spelled out.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: What good looks like (the real thing entrepreneurship teaches)
context: The slowest part of the journey is learning to recognise what good looks like at each level, in general and then for each specific role. He illustrates it with the private equity boardroom where he could see the gap between their team and his, which reset his bar for what talent even existed.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Broccoli wrapped in bacon (the valuable post)
context: Content that looks fun enough to pull people in but teaches something by the end. He contrasts the 'value post' (here are six things — nobody cares) with the valuable post (I did work, took risk or spent money for you): it is a bargain on the reader's time or money.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: Culture is the rules that govern reward and punishment
context: Every group has spoken and unspoken rules about what gets rewarded and what gets punished; those rules are the culture. Categories and pinned posts are how a community signals which behaviour it rewards, and pinning members' posts is the strongest possible signal.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday
claim: The guru model versus the network model of community
context: A community built as one-to-many relationships between you and every member breaks the moment you stop; a community where members are connected to each other survives you leaving because each member has several ties. One person can only have so many relationships, which is what caps the guru model.

title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

value: The $1,000 down converted to $16,000 collected in the first month, which he describes as making his LTV-to-CAC and acquisition cash flow 'super strong'. Clients averaged over $20,000 in additional new revenue in their first 30 days and moved from $36,000 to $112,000 in annual profit net of his fees. Early advertising returned 100 to 1. title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min
claim: Downside mitigation over upside
context: His stated allocation principle: because his upside is his business, he deliberately takes inferior returns on the money he parks, in exchange for knowing it will not go anywhere. He is buying the absence of downside, not the presence of return.

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min
claim: Make money on yourself twice

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min
claim: If you are financially done you must have a bigger purpose
context: Past a certain net worth money stops incrementally changing your life, so the work has to be meaningful in itself or there is nothing left to pursue. He frames the pursuit, not the outcome, as the source of purpose.

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min
claim: Right decisions can be wrong and wrong decisions can be right
context: Judge decisions on the information and criteria available at the time, not the outcome — otherwise you unlearn good habits that happened to lose and reinforce bad habits that happened to win.

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min
claim: Expanded time horizon (the reason the rich get richer)
context: Betting on a long enough horizon virtually removes risk, which makes guaranteed upside bets available to you. He says the rich get richer because their horizon lets them think this way, and the hardest thing is getting yourself into that perspective before you have the money.

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min

The number one KPI they track — excess cash flow — is the same thing the owner cares about.

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min

title: Big Business Owner Shares 1 YR of Wealth Lessons in 63min

context: Measuring yourself against an arbitrarily invented standard of happiness guarantees deficiency. Discarding the standard means any contentment you do find is above expectation, and the lower expectation also makes you improve faster.

title: I Confronted a Stranger With a Failing Business...
claim: A law firm for Latin-music artists and entrepreneurs (owner introduced as 'Alexi Omar' in the captions) with three units: legal services, education (courses/community), and a contract-template software product
value: No after-numbers - the video ends with the owner agreeing to the plan ('Will you do this? Yes.'). Hormozi's projections: $240,000 a month from the new-follower DM play alone, $18,000-$50,000 a day with three sellers at a $6,000 offer, and the next constraint becoming supply (running out of lawyers) rather than demand. He also says he does not know if the client will reach $1M a month from this.
context: Run the audit in this order: (1) kill or sell the unit that loses money - do not fund a fantasy while the cash runs out; (2) find where the money actually comes from today (here, unpromoted Instagram DMs) and point every existing traffic source at it instead of fixing the channel that never worked; (3) qualify hard before the sales call (budget, authority, need, timing) so the seller's time is only spent on people who can buy; (4) replace hourly pricing with outcome pricing and set a price anchor above it ($25,000 vs $5,800); (5) downsell everyone who does not qualify to a cheaper product at 4-6x its old checkout price, because a phone call typically triples what a page can charge; (6) enforce 80% gross margin on delivery. He summarises it as: you do not have to build anything new, you have to take what you already have and redirect it through a better monetization vehicle.

title: The first 5 hires EVERY entrepreneur should make...or go broke...
claim: His own portfolio companies (Acquisition.com, gym/fitness businesses) used as the reference case for sequencing the first hires
value: He claims the strategy of choosing financial debt over other debts is why each subsequent company grew bigger, faster and stronger than the ones before it, because they could skip the stages (new CRM, fixed financials, better management) that normally set a business back a quarter to a year.
context: Sequence your first hires by dollars-per-hour math, not by org chart: replace the cheapest, lowest-value-per-hour work first (admin, support), keep selling and marketing yourself while those are your highest-value hours, and take fractional help (bookkeeper, lawyer, tech) rather than in-house until scale justifies it. Then explicitly pick which debt to incur - paying for infrastructure and talent early (financial debt) is cheaper than paying back CRM, financial and management debt with interest later.

context: If you learn nothing from interviewing candidates for a role, you should not hire any of them - the interview process should teach you what you are missing.

title: I Built a Business That Runs Without Me
claim: Hormozi's own two fitness businesses inside the Acquisition.com portfolio - the worked example of active income becoming ownership income
value: He now does nothing in those two businesses. Profit went from $17M (2018) to a projected $8.1M this year with COVID for half the year, yet the businesses are 'more valuable now' than when he did everything. On a $8M base, a 20% return means going to $9.6M next year, which he calls ridiculously easy now that he can assemble rather than build.
context: Do not delegate one step at a time. At each step, hand over both the job you do now AND the next job you would have learned, to someone who already has that skill. You get the same growth curve the business had when you ran it, but you keep only the ownership. Corollary test: if you are the one doing the highest-value work in the business, you own a job, not a business - and your own skill level caps the business at the size you can personally run.

title: Building a $1,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 26 Minutes
claim: Optimum Works - Luis Lora's online railing store (homeowners, contractors, designers; 70% DIY, 30% custom orders; Shopify)
value: One year later (filming April 2025, follow-up March 2026): $3.6M revenue and $540,000 profit, +44% revenue growth. Custom orders went from 30% to 50% of the business - the single biggest driver of profit. Close rate is 20% with triple the number of custom-order leads submitted. Fixing attribution revealed campaigns that were only breaking even, so money was moved from losers to winners; prices were also raised. Owner's words: 'The advice that made the biggest difference was optimizing for custom orders and improving the custom orders page and improving the sales process.'
context: Fix the measurement before buying more traffic, and fix the customer mix before optimizing the funnel. Concretely: (1) if the reported LTV:CAC is arithmetically impossible for a profitable business, the attribution is broken and no spend decision is real - repair it and move budget to the campaigns that survive; (2) pick the segment you already have the most of that is least price sensitive and most obsessed, and re-aim the whole business at it instead of serving the most price-sensitive buyers who treat you as a commodity; (3) route every product through a one-step funnel (form + calendar, pre-call VSL, SMS BANT, close on the call with a card-vs-finance choice and a small on-call discount); (4) raise price where margins are thin and the segment does not care. Result to expect: mix shift toward the high-margin path (custom 30% to 50%), +44% revenue in a year.

title: I Blew Up A Secret Business To Prove It's Not Luck
claim: Ashley's fashion styling business - personal styling and design advice for high-income clients (CEOs, socialites, frequent flyers) with a $8,500 60-day onboarding, continuity, and 10% affiliate commission on clothing
value: No measured results are given in this video - the fixes are presented as a plan. His estimates: the funnel rebuild (lead magnet, VSSL, qualification, headline) could give her 2-3x, and if only 10% of clients take a high-end anchor priced at 10x, it effectively doubles the revenue of the business.
context: Three moves, in this order. (1) Before buying more traffic, stop the leak: give a narrow, qualified free thing, add a short pre-call video built from recorded objections, and qualify with BANT so unqualified people never consume your delivery time. (2) Hunt the gold mine already inside the business - find the channel that produced outsized results and do 10x more of it (here: 40 emails had produced 6 partners worth a third of revenue, so the instruction was 400 emails in 30 days, plus a relationship owner to keep partners activated). (3) Then reprice: add a high anchor about 10x the core price so the old top tier looks like a deal, make the back-end the default next step rather than a new pitch, and keep raising price while conversion holds.

title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview
claim: Shopify - the e-commerce platform Tobi Lütke started in 2005 and Harley Finkelstein joined, told here by Harley (third-party case study in an interview, not a Hormozi teardown)
value: IPO in May 2015 on the NYSE at about a $1 billion valuation - roughly 1% of today's market cap. In 2022 Shopify did $5.6 billion of revenue while its merchants generated almost $200 billion of GMV, and ecosystem partners earned more than $6 billion. By the time of this interview Shopify was worth around $100 billion with 8,000-9,000 employees. Harley's recurring finding from interviewing entrepreneurs in their 80s and 90s (about 12 interviews, including Izzy Sharp of Four Seasons at 95) is that they nearly all say the same thing: make your partners really rich.
context: Build the ecosystem, not just the product: give partners a reason to sell for you (80/20 rev share when the incumbent offered 70/30; 20% in perpetuity to referrers), run a competition that manufactures new customers and press before you can afford the prize, and use aggregate scale to negotiate rates your individual customers could never get. Two operating rules underneath it: one simple heuristic everyone can apply independently (merchant obsessed), and a decade-long time horizon (a 100-year business) that lets you refuse anything that is not a main quest. The check on whether you are doing it right: your partners should be making more money than you are.

title: We Broke The Guinness World Record In 24 Hours
claim: Acquisition.com's launch of the $100 Million Money Models book - a live 24-hour event with Guinness World Record judges present, selling the book for a $200 donation
value: The record was broken inside the 24-hour window - the Guinness judges confirmed they were the new official record holder, with the previous record at 1.43 million copies and the final number to be confirmed the next morning. Live milestones along the way: cracked 200,000, running at 1,000 books a second, $2M before lunch, past $3M, plus a single buyer taking 10,000 books for his community.
context: Make the claim and the proof the same object: if the offer is extraordinary, run the event that demonstrates it live rather than asserting it. Operationally, treat a one-shot launch as a pre-mortem exercise - enumerate the choke points in order (ad platforms, email/SMS sends, links, checkout), have a fallback chain for each (Google Ads to Meta to TikTok to LinkedIn), staff the checkout with humans, and rehearse the physical performance until it is automatic. The result here: an unknown-brand author beat Prince Harry's 1.4M-copy single-day record by having the launch itself be the evidence.

title: I Blew Up a Business Through 3 Small Changes (Just Copy Me)
claim: A music attorney (a solo/small legal practice serving musicians) whose clients come to him for a specific result - e.g. getting IP protection in place so their music can be sold to a record label.
value: No single closing revenue figure is given. Reported outcomes: the $100,000/year loss was the starting state; the price went from $250/hour to $5,800 upfront plus commission; traffic fixes were estimated to recover $20-50k/month that was already being generated but not routed. He notes the business was at stage four ('prioritize') of the scaling roadmap with 'product' as the constraint, and that the fix pattern (specialized product, V2 price to serve the new niche avatar, better free stuff, more creative volume, add qualification and friction) is the standard pattern for that stage.
context: Fix the three leaks in order: (1) kill whatever is losing money and eating the founder's hours, then push those hours into the one thing that already works; (2) find where customers already arrive by accident and put deliberate CTAs there - plus DM the followers you already have, opening with a two-option triage question ('free stuff or help?'); (3) replace time-based pricing with a flat fee priced against the result, and anchor it with a much higher zero-commission B offer and a slightly-cheaper DIY downsell so the core offer is obviously the best path. An exceptionally high close rate is not a win - it is the signal that you are underpriced.

title: "I'm Broke, What Business Do I Start?"

title: "I'm Broke, What Business Do I Start?"
claim: A registered dietitian who left a hospital job and now teaches other registered dietitians how to bill insurance - a business built from the Profession P.
value: She takes home almost a million dollars a year in income from a 5,800-follower Instagram account. No timeframe or revenue-vs-income breakdown is given.
context: The business comes from the workaround you were forced to invent, not from the job title. Take the narrowest specific process you had to figure out under pressure, and sell that process to the other people who have the same job and the same constraint - a 5,800-follower account was enough because the niche was narrow enough to command the price.

title: Can I Save This Failing Theme Park in 90 Days?
claim: Boulder Adventure Park - an indoor family entertainment centre in Grand Prairie, Texas, founded by Paul Fontinelli, who left corporate America eight years ago with three young kids. Revenue streams: general admission plus in-park spend (arcade, food and beverage, merchandise) making up about 70%, and group business (church groups, social groups, summer camps).
value: 3,700 leads in a local market (about 120/day), with between a third and half arriving in the final 48 hours. Summer camp revenue up 325% versus prior year. Admissions doubled over four to six weeks once Hormozi's own video clips were used as ads. But the close rate suffered: the three-person sales team could not call the leads fast enough, and Paul says the result could have been much higher with proper manpower and a call sequence. Hormozi's verdict: the intervention bought Paul roughly three more months of life if he executed everything, and the same play should be re-run for birthdays. Paul's own 401k went in.
context: When a business is weeks from death, do not fix the business - buy time. Pick the single highest-cash offer available inside the current seasonal window, run it as a short prize-led giveaway with a hard countdown and a 72-hour claim window, and make sure the second-place prize lands exactly on your core paid offer so the giveaway pre-sells it. Model the final 48 hours as a third to a half of all leads regardless of campaign length. Then repeat the identical play in a cheaper, year-round version (here: birthdays) - and fix the sales capacity before the leads arrive, because in this teardown the offer worked and the close rate was the thing that leaked.

title: Helping a Stranger Build A $15,000,000/yr Business in 32 Minutes
claim: Precision Health Concierge Medicine - a concierge/optimisation medical practice in Sarasota, Florida, owned by Dr. Zad Oasi (CEO), with a founding partner as medical director. Members pay an annual fee; revenue is augmented by aesthetics treatments, supplementation, and an expensive body scan. The practice is 16 people.
value: No revenue result is reported inside the session. Hormozi's model: a 300-person event yields scans on a third (~100 scans), 25% conversion yields 25 sales, which at the practice's LTV is about a $2.5M event - and he sets a target of $200,000-$400,000 from 10 events in one quarter, which would pace the practice to $10M+ by year end. He predicts this will be the business of those he looked at that generates the most money in the shortest time, and rates it 'scaling'. The owner's own 90-day update at the end contradicts part of the plan: he did not run Hormozi's event play. Sarasota shuts down May-September with half the population leaving, so he could not find suitable third-party events; instead of attending events he built his own lecture series with venues where his ideal clients live - explicitly the thing Hormozi had told him not to do. He reports inbound interest from appearing on the show, and no financial figures.
context: For a high-trust, high-ticket service, do not start with cold paid traffic - classify your process as warm or cold first. Then attach the referral request to the touchpoints that already exist (at the close, and at every treatment) and reframe it from 'refer a friend' to 'who do you want to bring with you?', backed by a perk with real face value that is only available to referrals. Finally, if you have an expensive diagnostic or assessment, use it as the sales window itself: run the video sales letter while the customer is being scanned, and close the moment it ends.

title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes
claim: Proshine Professional Cleaning - an HVAC cleaning and duct work repair company in the Hilton Head / Bluffton area, run by Corey and his wife Nicole. Core services: HVAC duct cleaning at $1,575/unit with a 2-year growth-free guarantee, duct work re-wrapping, and dryer vent cleaning at $175. A large share of business comes from affiliate referrals from HVAC, pest control and remediation companies.
value: One-year check-in: revenue moved from $1.25M trailing to a $2.3M-$2.5M run rate, with Hormozi summarising it as 'almost doubled within a year'. Lead flow went from about 120/month to about 200/month, with higher quality leads. Corey attributes the biggest impact to marketing: they replaced the third-party agency with one that had done it for other companies, and made the landing page conversions, marketing changes and ad spend increases. He is planning another location in the next 12 months. Profit projections given in the session were 25% up from pricing and 5% more once debt is cleared; the plan was estimated at roughly 25% profit increase plus 2x from page optimisation, 2-3x from ads/organic, 10-20% from retargeting and 20-30% from email reactivation.
context: With a healthy, high-margin business the move is incremental, not a rebuild: raise price to the point where the close rate would have to fall below a stated floor for it to lose money (an 80%+ close rate is the signal), then fix the funnel and the creative BEFORE adding spend, because a page that converts and ads that read at mobile size may multiply lead flow for free. Then stack the compounding layers in order: retargeting, your own branded search terms, a reactivation email campaign framed as 'we owe you' rather than 'we're back', and finally a real affiliate programme where the partner keeps 100% of a low-ticket high-margin item you deliver - your CAC becomes delivery cost divided by the upsell rate.

title: Building a $5,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 42 Mins
claim: ChiroFirst of Washington (as stated in the caption - 'Kyo first of Washington'), a six-location chiropractic chain founded by Raymond Coer. Services: custom treatment plans of chiropractic, rehab and spinal decompression over 60-90 days, with spinal decompression as the differentiator. 75% insurance, 25% cash. All six locations were acquired rather than opened organically.
value: No result is reported inside the session - the video ends with the plan. Hormozi's projections: an easy 2x in lead flow from the ad copy and lead magnet changes; plus 10% from reordering the same-day sale; local SEO worth 30-50% but taking about a year; and about a 20% lift from the sales process changes. He estimates that doubling revenue across the existing locations would already put the business at $5M EBITDA without opening another store, since fixed costs stay roughly the same. Total implementation time: about six months of work. He rates the business as strong ('Raymond was amazing') and notes the owner is on level six of the scaling roadmap, needing better sales training, individual coaching and a team cadence to graduate.
context: When the same model produces different results at different locations, the lever is the people, not the model - so pick interventions with low operational risk. Then look for the two signs that money is being left on the table: a close rate far above the healthy 30-40% band (you are underpriced) and a measured ROAS of 10:1 or better on a channel you are barely funding (you are under-spent; efficiency will fall as you scale and that is fine, down to about a 5:1 floor). Finally, check WHEN you ask for the sale: if you relieve the pain before you present the price, you are selling at the point of greatest satisfaction and you will lose most of the sale - sell at the point of greatest pain, and take a card up front so the customer actually arrives.

title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes
claim: Bashu & Co Thai Cuisine (also captioned 'Basil and Co') in Diamond Bar, California - a Thai restaurant run by husband-and-wife owners Calvin and Air, who met 15 years ago as a buser and a server in a Santa Monica Thai restaurant. 72 seats, mid-to-high income neighbourhood, mid-priced menu. Second location, a 100-seat restaurant with a bigger bar, opening in Arcadia, California.
value: No outcome is reported - the video ends at the prioritised plan. Hormozi's own projections, stated separately and not additive: the 99-cent change alone is +30% profit with no change in sales velocity; reordering the menu by gross profit is 10-20%; the alcohol and pairing changes are the one he feels best about at 40%+; first-timer training is about 10%, worth $300,000-$400,000/year at their revenue and more important for location two; the manager-card review mechanic is about a 20% lift. His summary is that the three that will move the needle most are cheap and can be implemented over a weekend - the owners say they can do it in a night.
context: In a high-volume, thin-margin business the leverage is in cents, not strategy: a 99-cent reprice on a $16 item is 6% of revenue and 30% of profit, and reordering a menu by gross profit costs nothing. Look for the highest-margin line you already sell but barely sell (here alcohol at 1% against a 5-15% industry standard), then remove the friction for the customer and the memory burden for the staff - print the pairing under the dish, put one item on the table, give the server a scripted sentence and a reason of their own to say it. Engineer the ending of the experience (surprise dessert via the manager's own card, not a coupon), and ask for reviews at the point of sale in exchange for something immediate, because 'next time' gets paid instead.

title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 57 Mins
claim: Unfiltered Hospitality - a bar and beverage program consultancy co-founded by Ben (ex-investment banker, ex-bar owner) and his business partner Ghee. Clients are restaurants, hotels, bars, country clubs, cruise ships and nightclubs. Two products: 'better cocktail consulting' (phase one, 90 days - design the cocktail menu, train the team, install the operating system) and the 'program performance retainer' (phase two - weekly KPI scorecard call, seasonal monthly cocktails, quarterly 2-day on-site team training).
value: No outcome is reported - the video ends at the plan. Hormozi's projections, stated separately and not additive: the funnel redo alone could triple lead volume; ad call outs could 2-3x click-through; landing page conversion could go from 7% to about 30% (a 4x); close rate from 6% to 30-50%; upsell rate to at least 50% against today's less than 20%; and founder selling alone would be 'more than a 5x in sales'. At a 30% close rate he says Ben would make the same revenue on the front end alone, without the $30,000 back end, and at 50% he would make 40% more revenue with the back end still intact. He explicitly states these are 'high likely shots', not guarantees.
context: When a premium offer will not sell, check the timing before the price: a $30,000 engagement sold cold to strangers is the wrong offer at the wrong time, no matter how good it is. Insert a lead magnet between cold traffic and the sale to move people from low trust to high trust, then build a front-end offer at roughly a fifth of the price that solves one narrow problem so well it produces ten times its cost - and roll that payment into the back end rather than discounting it. Spread the rollover credit over four quarters, not the first payment, so you get commitment rather than an easy yes. Fix churn before buying more traffic, because a leaky bucket wastes everything upstream. And until the founder physically cannot, the founder should be the one on the calls.

title: He Makes $600,000,000/Yr Selling Bacon
claim: CustomMade.com - a marketplace connecting customers to woodworkers and makers for custom pieces (custom coffee tables, custom jewellery). Bought in 2008 by Mike Salguero and his best friend Seth out of their real-estate jobs, and later repositioned as a venture-backed marketplace.
value: Failure. Eight years (2008-2015) with nothing to show: GMV peaked around $3-4M/month but take rate was about 7% (roughly $200,000/month) while burn at its height was $500,000/month. Mike's ownership was diluted to about 8% and he had 'a good salary' but no outcome. The company was foreclosed on by its venture-debt lender. 50 people were let go, and Mike let go of the friends who had built the company with him. He describes sitting in his car in the parking lot unable to go into the office. His takeaways: do not take investment, he lost his team and lost himself.
context: Do not raise on a story that is not your actual business - once investors buy the narrative you can no longer pivot away from it, even when the model is unworkable. And model the unit economics of the middle: standing between two parties to take a fee only works if the transaction is simple, and here each sale required dozens of exchanges to earn a 7% cut. The counterfactual Mike and Hormozi both draw is that the bootstrapped version - $35,000/year to $60,000/month, nearly profitable - was the better business, and the capital destroyed it.

title: He Makes $600,000,000/Yr Selling Bacon
claim: ButcherBox - a direct-to-consumer meat subscription shipping grass-fed beef, chicken, pork and seafood. Founded by Mike Salguero in September 2015, one weekend after closing CustomMade. Bootstrapped, profitable from day one, and still owning its own backbone only partially: no farms, no slaughterhouses, no distribution - the only owned piece is two dry-ice plants.
value: Revenue went from about $200,000 in the Kickstarter to roughly $500,000, then $5M, $33M, $105M, $220M, then $450M in the COVID year, with $450M, $550M and $570M in the following years, before the first down year in 2023 and a return to about 6% growth. Mike owns 70% and has bought back $20-30M of shares from early holders. The business has 430,000 customers, churns about 3%/month, retains about 60% of first-year customers, has an NPS of 63, has shipped to 1.7-1.75 million households, and runs at about a 30% gross margin and about 6% net margin. Headcount was over-corrected from 85 to a peak of 240 (with 85 managers) and has been brought back to about 195. No outcome is given for the interventions Hormozi proposes at the end (pushing the cooking content public), because the conversation ends with the suggestion.
context: Fund the business with the customer's money, not an investor's: pre-sell, then reverse-engineer whatever mechanic gives you free reach (here the Kickstarter verified badge), and add a stretch-goal bonus so buyers promote for you. Then do the unscalable work that actually creates the first cohort - ship fast, phone every buyer, handwrite the cards - and buy your way out of the work you personally will not do. Build your outreach list by reverse-engineering a bigger competitor's partner page. Pay affiliates in commissions for life rather than upfront, because you have no money and they want recurring income. Turn your best one-time bonus into a lifetime one, because it lowers effective CAC below the cost of the item and makes leaving expensive. And own only the one thing whose failure zeroes your revenue - for a frozen-meat business, that is dry ice.

claim: Garby Disposal Services — residential trash, recycling and yard waste collection in Centreville/Chantilly/Clifton/Fairfax, Virginia. Owner: Philip. Two customer avatars (scatter/residential and HOAs) and four-plus acquisition channels (door-to-door, Meta ads, cold email, handwritten letters, referrals).
value: Not reported in this video — the session ends with the plan and a prioritized recap. Hormozi's projections inside the conversation: with 10 reps at 5 sales/day that is 50 sales/day and 1,500 sales/month (which he says overshoots the goal by ~8x); with just the owner plus one rep doing 10 deals/day they would be at 300/month, hitting the extra 1,000 customers within about 3 months. Outcome stated as: cash flow positive.
context: When a business is unprofitable but the unit economics are actually fine (18:1 and 21:1 LTV:CAC), the constraint is almost never leads or margin — it is the timing of cash. Compute the exact fully-loaded cost of acquiring and setting up one customer (COGS-to-first-payment + CAC + commission), then redesign the OFFER so that average upfront cash collected exceeds that number, using an anchor option at the top rather than raising the core price. Anchors work on blended averages: if even 20% take the higher-commitment option, the average per-unit cash rises enough to fund growth debt-free, and you never need a financing partner. Simultaneously collapse the choice set — one avatar, one channel — because a small business spread across two avatars and five channels cannot execute any of them at the volume required. And when the asset you're giving away is what the customer actually needs (the bin), stop discounting it to zero: price it, or trade it for commitment.

claim: Trophy Outlet (trophyoutlet.com) — custom trophies, awards and personalization, plus a separate gag-gift brand (funny signs, 'head mofo in charge' style gifts) sold on Amazon, Etsy and TikTok Shop. Third-generation family business, started 1985 (40th year), one retail location plus one production facility, ~$1.72M revenue. Owner: Cody Schulson.
value: Not reported in this video — it ends with a 9-item prioritized plan and the owner's reaction ('much cleaner and simpler than I thought'). Modelled impacts stated during the session: price test = 2x profit on its own (potentially 4-5x if he can push 25%); closing the location = +50% profit; SEO max-out = ~50% revenue boost; PPC = 10-20% boost; email = ~$1.5M sitting unused; TikTok mastery = the lever from $1M to $10M.
context: When a business is profitable but barely, check the PRICE before the funnel. The diagnostic test: if the highest-quality, zero-acquisition-cost segment (word-of-mouth return customers) is still not making you rich, and your fixed costs are not high, you are mispriced — full stop. Pricing is the highest-return, lowest-drag lever available (you change a number, not a process), and at single-digit net margins a 6% price increase is roughly a 100% profit increase. So: run rolling small price tests on your highest-velocity SKUs, optimize gross profit x units sold rather than conversion rate, and expect to make more money before you make less. In parallel, stop paying attention to things with no strategic advantage — shut the location that doesn't break even (a cost cut at single-digit margins is worth more than a revenue initiative), pick one of your two businesses, and double down on the channel that is already returning 13:1 rather than diversifying into unproven ones. Finally, treat the first sale as customer acquisition and build the repeat path deliberately: an in-box offer, behavioural email flows, and a weekly nurture email — the return customers you are currently getting by accident can be tripled by design.

claim: Autobiographical — his own escape from poverty and the business trajectory that followed (personal training -> gyms -> licensing -> acquisition.com). Not a stranger's teardown; the 'case' is his own.
value: First $100,000 took 5 years, saved $1 at a time. Six gyms by age 26, all cash-flowed. Licensing business at $4 million/month. Later, the people asking him for help escalated with each tier (personal training clients -> gym owners -> licensing operators -> large-business owners), which is the ladder that produced his consulting and content business.
context: The order matters and the first step is psychological, not tactical: you cannot change a situation you are still blaming on something else, because blame is where you hand over your power. So the sequence is (1) own it entirely, (2) use whatever fuel you actually have — anger and shame work as well as passion — (3) take only the next step, never plan the whole path, (4) spend less than you make and put every excess dollar into skills rather than into feeling better or looking better, and (5) treat failed experiments as experience points rather than losses. Two reusable heuristics carry the rest: the friend test (does this person increase or decrease the probability of hitting my goal — there is no in-between), and future pacing (make the pain of staying the same exceed the pain of changing). And the meta-lesson on authority: don't sell advice on something you have not done — accumulate evidence first and let people come and ask, which is how the ladder from trainer to gym owner to licensing operator to large-business advisor actually got built.

claim: Mim Jenkinson's sticker-teaching business — she teaches crafters how to make stickers. Low-ticket digital products with a main membership (Secret Sticker Society, $27/month or $217/year) and many interchangeable low-ticket upsells. Acquisition runs through a live paid bootcamp launched three times a year. 20,000+ crafters taught over 10 years. Two employees (one is her husband).
value: Verdict delivered in-video: 'you will be scaling with me.' No revenue result yet — she reports early-stage promotion for the next launch moving in the right direction, and confirms the previous piece of advice (pitching annual) doubled her average cart value. Hormozi's stated view: very few universes where adding the physical premium and presenting annual-only does not generate more revenue up front, and the plan has the potential to 5x or 10x the business.
context: When the product and retention already work (22% conversion, 5% churn, 30-35% margins) and delivery does not break when you double volume, the constraint is never the product — it is that the owner has capped their own inputs. Three inputs to un-cap in order: (1) SPEND — if you are highly profitable and your CPA has never once exceeded $50, a self-imposed cap is pure fear, not strategy; set a CPA ceiling you are willing to pay and then actually pay it. (2) CREATIVE VOLUME — the account needs hundreds of ads, not four. Generate them from assets you already own: re-shoot your 20 all-time winners in four settings, clip every live session, screenshot the community, and build an activation so every new customer produces an ad. (3) SPEND CADENCE — do not spread budget evenly; test cheap in week one, then put the majority of the budget into the final three days of the event. Then fix the OFFER so the cash arrives sooner: remove the cheaper option that cannibalizes the premium one, attach a physical premium to the annual instead of discounting it, and use a high-priced bundle as a decoy to make the annual obvious. The most reusable move is the last one: instead of selling a $10 ticket and converting 22% of buyers, sell the event AS a trial of the membership — front-end conversion goes to 100% because everyone must actively cancel, and the entire event becomes an annual-selling machine.

claim: Scaling the unscalable

claim: The done-for-you / done-with-you / do-it-yourself pyramid (the Tesla model)
context: Start at the TOP of the pyramid with the most expensive, done-for-you offer. You have few customers so maximise revenue per customer, you get the best results, and you develop the SOPs and productised assets that let you move downstream later. Then step down to done-with-you (a third to a fifth of the price) and finally DIY (a tenth), selling 10x the people at a tenth of the handholding.

title: Stop Being Broke. Get Busy.
